$$\newcommand{\nimplies}{\mathrel{\rlap{\mkern 20mu /}\implies}}$$

# Separation Axiom
## Definition
Let $(X, \mathscr{T})$ be a topological space. 

**(i)** $X$ is called a ***$T_0$-space*** if for all $x, y \in X$ with $x \neq y$, $\exists U \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $x \in U$ and $y \notin U$.

**(ii)** $X$ is called a ***$T_1$-space*** if for all $x, y \in X$ with $x \neq y$, $\exists U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $x \in U, y \notin U$ and $y \in V, x \notin V$.

**(iii)** $X$ is called a ***$T_2$-space*** or ***Hausdorff space*** if for all $x, y \in X$ with $x \neq y$, $\exists U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $x \in U, y \in V$ and $U \cap V = \emptyset$.

**(iv)** $X$ is called a ***regular space*** if for a closed subset $C$ of $X$ and $x \notin C$, $\exists U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $x \in U, C \subset V$ and $U \cap V = \emptyset$.

**(v)** $X$ is called a ***$T_3$-space*** or ***regular Hausdorff*** if $X$ is regular and $T_1$.

**(vi)** $X$ is called a ***normal space*** if for closed subsets $C, D$ of $X$ with $C \cap D = \emptyset$, $\exists U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $C \subset U, D \subset V$ and $U \cap V = \emptyset$.

**(vii)** $X$ is called a ***$T_4$-space*** or ***normal Hausdorff*** if $X$ is normal and $T_1$.

## Example
**(i)** $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$ is a $T_4$-space. 

**(ii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_c)$ is a $T_1$-space, but not a $T_2$-space.

**(iii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_K)$ is a $T_2$-space, but not a $T_3$-space.

## Remark 1
**(i)** $T_4 \implies T_3 \implies T_2 \implies T_1 \implies T_0$

**(ii)** "Regular" $\nimplies$ "Hausdorff"

$\big[ (\because)$ Let $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $\mathscr{T} = \{ \emptyset, \{ 1, 2 \}, \{ 3, 4 \}, X \}$. Then $(X, \mathscr{T})$ is regular, but it is not Hausdorff. For $1 \neq 2$, there are no open sets $U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $1 \in U, 2 \in V$ and $U \cap V = \emptyset$. $\big]$

**(iii)** "Normal" $\nimplies$ "Regular"

$\big[ (\because)$ Let $X = \{1, 2\}$ and $\mathscr{T} = \{ \emptyset, \{ 1 \}, X \}$. Then $(X, \mathscr{T})$ is normal, but it is not regular. For $1 \in X$ and closed set $\{ 2 \}$, there are no open sets $U, V \in \mathscr{T}$ such that $1 \in U, \{ 2 \} \subset V$ and $U \cap V = \emptyset$. $\big]$

## Theorem 1
Let $\mathscr{T}$ and $\mathscr{T}'$ be two topological space on a set $X$. Suppose that $\mathscr{T} \subset \mathscr{T}'$. 

**(i)** If $\mathscr{T}$ is $T_0$, then $\mathscr{T}'$ is $T_0$.

**(ii)** If $\mathscr{T}$ is $T_1$, then $\mathscr{T}'$ is $T_1$.

**(iii)** If $\mathscr{T}$ is $T_2$, then $\mathscr{T}'$ is $T_2$.

### Proof

## Lemma
Let $X$ be a $T_1$ space.

**(i)** $X$ is regular $\iff$ for each $x \in X$ and an open set $U$ with $x \in U$, there exists an open set $V$ in $X$ such that $x \in V$ and $\overline{V} \subset U$.

**(ii)** $X$ is normal $\iff$ for each closed set $C$ of $X$ and an open set $U$ in $X$ with $C \subset U$, there exists an open set $V$ in $X$ such that $C \subset V$ and $\overline{V} \subset U$.

### Proof

## Theorem 2
**(i)** A subspace of a $T_3$ space is $T_3$.

**(ii)** The product space of $T_3$ spaces is $T_3$.

### Proof

## Remark 2
We cannot generalize this theorem to $T_4$ spaces. That is,

**(i)** A subspace of a $T_4$ space is not necessarily $T_4$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" collapse="true" icon=false}

:::

**(ii)** The product space of $T_4$ spaces is not necessarily $T_4$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" collapse="true" icon=false}

:::
